steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a web privacy paper presenting Purl, a machine-learning approach that removes just the tracking information from decorated links. Cover why current anti-tracking tools fall short, our key insight, how Purl works, the evaluation and measurement results, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Arms race between anti-tracking tools and trackers
- Key insight: block the sharing of tracking information; link decoration and the granularity problem
- Current link decoration sanitization relies on manual lists
- Purl: approach
- Evaluation and measurement results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Arms race
  - browsers/extensions cracking down on new tracking techniques
  - mainstream browsers block or will block third-party cookies; privacy-focused browsers counter browser fingerprinting
  - trackers evolve to bypass countermeasures
  - limitation: tools target specific tracking types (third-party cookies, first-party cookies, email addresses, canvas fingerprinting, AudioContext fingerprinting, CNAME cloaking); fail on new/unknown forms
- Key insight
  - trackers must share info (user/device identifiers) client -> server regardless of technique
  - orthogonal approach: detect and block sharing of tracking info in network requests
  - tracking info put in "decorated" request URLs (link decoration)
  - existing tools block whole requests via filter lists of known trackers
  - decorated link mixes tracking and functional info (CSRF tokens, news/product subpages) -> block breaks functionality, allow leaks tracking
  - granularity issue; unmet need for fine-grained removal
- Manual sanitization
  - Safari, Firefox, Brave, uBlock Origin, AdGuard: manually-curated lists of tracking query parameters; like EasyList, EasyPrivacy
  - can't keep pace with trackers' growing use of query parameters; same problem hit filter lists
  - lists target only 10-100s of parameters
- Purl
  - pronounced purel-l; ML to tell tracking from functional link decorations
  - cross-layer graph of full page execution: HTML DOM, JavaScript execution, browser storage, network requests
  - features from graph + supervised classifier
- Results
  - top-million sample: 98.87% recall, 98.62% precision, 98.74% accuracy
  - beats existing countermeasures by at least 7.71% precision, 4.83% recall, 6.43% accuracy; breakage reduced by more than 8 \times
  - robust to evasion: renaming decorations, splitting/combining values
  - deployment on subset of top-million: 73.02% of sites abuse link decorations, average 10.75 tracking decorations per site
  - top abusers: advertising and tracking services sharing cookies, email addresses, fingerprinting info
- Contributions: (1) Purl, cross-layer features; (2) measurement of prevalence, abusers, type of info; (3) filter list already used by privacy-focused browsers/extensions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Web browsers and browser extensions are actively cracking down on new and emerging online tracking techniques. For example, almost all mainstream web browsers already block third-party cookies or will soon block them, and some privacy-focused browsers even deploy countermeasures against emerging tracking techniques like browser fingerprinting. As a response, online trackers keep evolving and they come up with innovative tracking techniques which can bypass the existing privacy-enhancing countermeasures. The main limitation of existing privacy-enhancing tools is that they try to mitigate specific types of tracking (e.g., third-party cookies, first-party cookies, email addresses, canvas fingerprinting, AudioContext fingerprinting, CNAME cloaking). This works reasonably well against known forms of tracking but it fails against new or unknown forms of tracking, and these emerge routinely from time to time.

Our key insight is that trackers need to share information (e.g., user/device identifiers) from the client to the server side no matter what type of tracking they use. So we think a promising orthogonal approach to anti-tracking is to detect and block the sharing of tracking information in network requests. Trackers commonly put tracking information into "decorated" network request URLs (aka link decoration). Existing privacy-enhancing tools block network requests outright, using filter lists of known tracking services. But a decorated link can include both tracking information (e.g., user/device identifiers) and functional information (e.g., CSRF tokens, identifying news/product subpages), and so the existing request blocking countermeasures are ineffective – if they block the request they risk breaking legitimate functionality as collateral damage, and if they don't block it they risk allowing privacy-invasive tracking. Basically this is a granularity issue. To the best of our knowledge, there is an unmet need for a fine-grained approach that can remove exactly the tracking information in decorated links.

To sanitize link decoration (i.e., to remove just the tracking information from a request URL), privacy-focused browsers and browser extensions like Safari, Firefox, Brave, uBlock Origin, and AdGuard use a manually-curated list of query parameters that are known to be abused for tracking, similar to the request-blocking filter lists like EasyList and EasyPrivacy. The manual approach might work for a small number of tracking query parameters, but it cannot keep up with the increasing adoption of query parameters by trackers, which is a problem that has also badly impacted filter lists. So it is not surprising that the filter lists for sanitizing link decoration conservatively target only 10-100s of query parameters.

- Purl: ML approach (pronounced purel-l); cross-layer graph (HTML DOM, JavaScript execution, browser storage, network requests); features + supervised classifier
- Results: 98.87% recall, 98.62% precision, 98.74% accuracy; beats existing countermeasures by at least 7.71% / 4.83% / 6.43%; breakage reduced more than 8 \times; robust to evasion
- Deployment: 73.02% of sites, 10.75 tracking decorations on average; advertising and tracking services share cookies, email addresses, fingerprinting info
- Contributions: Purl; measurement; filter list already in use

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Web browsers and browser extensions are actively cracking down on new and emerging online tracking techniques. For example, almost all mainstream web browsers already block third-party cookies or will soon block them, and some privacy-focused browsers even deploy countermeasures against emerging tracking techniques like browser fingerprinting. As a response, online trackers keep evolving and they come up with innovative tracking techniques which can bypass the existing privacy-enhancing countermeasures. The main limitation of existing privacy-enhancing tools is that they try to mitigate specific types of tracking (e.g., third-party cookies, first-party cookies, email addresses, canvas fingerprinting, AudioContext fingerprinting, CNAME cloaking). This works reasonably well against known forms of tracking but it fails against new or unknown forms of tracking, and these emerge routinely from time to time.

Our key insight is that trackers need to share information (e.g., user/device identifiers) from the client to the server side no matter what type of tracking they use. So we think a promising orthogonal approach to anti-tracking is to detect and block the sharing of tracking information in network requests. Trackers commonly put tracking information into "decorated" network request URLs (aka link decoration). Existing privacy-enhancing tools block network requests outright, using filter lists of known tracking services. But a decorated link can include both tracking information (e.g., user/device identifiers) and functional information (e.g., CSRF tokens, identifying news/product subpages), and so the existing request blocking countermeasures are ineffective – if they block the request they risk breaking legitimate functionality as collateral damage, and if they don't block it they risk allowing privacy-invasive tracking. Basically this is a granularity issue. To the best of our knowledge, there is an unmet need for a fine-grained approach that can remove exactly the tracking information in decorated links.

To sanitize link decoration (i.e., to remove just the tracking information from a request URL), privacy-focused browsers and browser extensions like Safari, Firefox, Brave, uBlock Origin, and AdGuard use a manually-curated list of query parameters that are known to be abused for tracking, similar to the request-blocking filter lists like EasyList and EasyPrivacy. The manual approach might work for a small number of tracking query parameters, but it cannot keep up with the increasing adoption of query parameters by trackers, which is a problem that has also badly impacted filter lists. So it is not surprising that the filter lists for sanitizing link decoration conservatively target only 10-100s of query parameters.

In this paper, we propose Purl (pronounced purel-l), which is a machine-learning approach for telling apart tracking and functional link decorations. Purl uses a cross-layer graph representation that captures the complete execution of a webpage, including the interactions between the HTML DOM structure, the JavaScript execution behavior, the information stored in browser storage, and the network requests issued while the webpage loads. Then Purl extracts distinguishing features from this graph representation and it uses a supervised classifier to detect tracking link decorations.

We evaluated Purl on a sample of top-million websites and it can sanitize link decoration effectively (98.87% recall) and safely (98.62% precision). Overall Purl gets 98.74% accuracy. It is significantly better than existing countermeasures, by at least 7.71% in precision, 4.83% in recall, and 6.43% in overall accuracy, and it reduces website breakage by more than 8 \times. The evaluation also shows that Purl is robust against common evasion attempts like changing the names of link decorations and splitting/combining link decoration values.

We also deploy Purl on a subset of top-million websites to measure how prevalent link decorations for tracking are. Purl detects that 73.02% of the sites abuse link decorations for tracking, and an average site uses 10.75 tracking link decorations. We find that the most common abusers of link decoration are well-known advertising and tracking services, and they use link decorations to share cookies, email addresses, and fingerprinting information.

Our key contributions are:

1. We propose and evaluate an automated machine learning approach, called Purl, that detects tracking link decorations using features which capture the interactions and flow of information across multiple layers of the web stack.

2. We deploy Purl on top-million sites to measure the prevalence, the abusers, and the type of tracking information that is shared via link decorations.

3. We use Purl to generate a filter list, which can be used, and is already being used, by privacy-focused browsers and browser extensions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Web browsers and browser extensions are actively cracking down on new and emerging online tracking techniques. For example, almost all mainstream web browsers now already block or will soon block third-party cookies [1,2,3], and some privacy-focused browsers even deploy countermeasures against emerging tracking techniques, such as browser fingerprinting [4,5,6]. In response, online trackers continue to evolve and devise innovative tracking techniques that can bypass existing privacy-enhancing countermeasures [7,8,9,10]. The key limitation of existing privacy-enhancing tools is that they aim to mitigate specific types of tracking (e.g., third-party cookies, first-party cookies, email addresses, canvas fingerprinting, AudioContext fingerprinting, CNAME cloaking) [11,12,8,13]. Our key insight is that trackers need to share information (e.g., user/device identifiers) from the client to the server side regardless of the type of tracking employed. Therefore, we contend that a promising orthogonal approach to anti-tracking is to detect and block the sharing of tracking information in network requests. Trackers commonly include tracking information in "decorated" network request URLs (aka link decoration). Existing privacy-enhancing tools outright block network requests to endpoints using filter lists of known tracking services. However, a decorated link can include both tracking (e.g., user/device identifiers) and functional (e.g., CSRF tokens, identifying news/product subpages) information, which renders existing request blocking countermeasures ineffective – they risk breaking legitimate functionality as collateral damage if they block the request, and risk allowing privacy-invasive tracking if they do not. This is fundamentally a granularity issue. To the best of our knowledge, there is an unmet need for a fine-grained approach that can precisely remove tracking information in decorated links.

To sanitize link decoration (i.e., to precisely remove just the tracking information from a request URL), privacy-focused browsers and browser extensions such as Safari, Firefox, Brave, uBlock Origin, and AdGuard employ a manually-curated list of query parameters known to be abused for tracking [16,17,18,19,20], similar to request-blocking filter lists such as EasyList and EasyPrivacy [21,22]. It is thus not surprising that the filter lists to sanitize link decoration conservatively target only 10-100s of query parameters.

In this paper, we propose Purl (pronounced purel-l), a machine-learning approach to distinguish between tracking and functional link decorations. Purl uses a cross-layer graph representation to capture the complete execution of a webpage, including interactions between the HTML DOM structure, JavaScript execution behavior, information stored in browser storage, and network requests issued during a webpage load. Purl then extracts distinguishing features from this rich graph representation and uses a supervised classifier to detect tracking link decorations.

Our evaluation on a sample of top-million websites shows that Purl can effectively (98.87% recall) and safely (98.62% precision) sanitize link decoration. Overall, Purl achieves 98.74% accuracy, significantly outperforming existing countermeasures by at least 7.71% in precision, 4.83% in recall, and 6.43% in overall accuracy, while reducing website breakage by more than 8 \times. Our evaluation also shows that Purl is robust against common evasion attempts such as changing link decoration names and splitting/combining link decoration values.

We deploy Purl on a subset of top-million websites to measure the prevalence of link decorations for tracking. Purl detects that 73.02% of the sites abuse link decorations for tracking, with an average site using 10.75 tracking link decorations. We find that the most common abusers of link decoration include well-known advertising and tracking services, which use link decorations to share cookies, email addresses, and fingerprinting information.

Our key contributions are as follows:

1. We propose and evaluate an automated machine learning approach, called Purl, to detect tracking link decorations using features that capture interactions and the flow of information across multiple layers of the web stack.

2. We deploy Purl on top-million sites to measure the prevalence, abusers, and type of tracking information shared via link decorations.

3. We use Purl to generate a filter list, which can be and is already being used by privacy-focused browsers and browser extensions.
